title: Je vais déjeuner deux fois  (I'll Have Lunch Twice)

segments.t: Last time, Cécile de France turned up late to a photo shoot, still smelling of her horse-riding lesson, and her agent Gabriel learned by message that Tarantino doesn't want her because of her age. He kept it to himself. Now it's morning at the agency in Paris. The doors open, the phones start ringing, and we follow Andréa, the toughest and fastest-talking agent at ASK, as she rushes in with her assistant Magali reading out her diary. Mathias, a smooth, ambitious agent, is already on the phone talking money. Here it is in French first. Don't worry about catching every word.
Bonjour! Salut, Mathias.
Oui, trois cent mille. Je parle de ses vingt ans de carrière.
Magali, je dois voir la pièce de Koltès cette semaine.
Deux places pour mardi? Mardi, tu as le film de Kechiche.
Jeudi, alors.
Et demain, tu déjeunes avec Audiard.
Je prends ça. Merci.
Tu déjeunes aussi avec Dany Boon demain.
Tu es pénible, Magali.
L'un à midi, l'autre à quatorze heures. Je vais déjeuner deux fois.
Appelle Clémentine. Dis-lui que je ne peux pas venir ce soir.
Clémentine? Celle de la semaine dernière?
Il y a une autre Clémentine?
Qu'est-ce que je lui dis?
Je ne sais pas. Trouve quelque chose.
Dis que j'ai une réunion. Improvise!
Gabriel. Tu ne rappelles pas Cécile de France?
Let's take it apart. Andréa sweeps in through the door, greeting everyone in one breath, while Mathias barely looks up from his call.
Bonjour! Salut, Mathias.
'Morning! Hi, Mathias.' The first word is the all-purpose greeting; the second is the casual hello you use with people you know well. Colleagues here are all on first-name terms.
Oui, trois cent mille.
'Yes, three hundred thousand.' Mathias is negotiating a fee for an actor, and he doesn't waste words.
Je parle de ses vingt ans de carrière.
'I'm talking about his twenty years of career.' In other words: you're not paying for twenty days of filming, you're paying for twenty years of being a star.
Magali, je dois voir la pièce de Koltès cette semaine.
'Magali, I have to see the Koltès play this week.' The verb for 'have to' comes first, then the plain verb 'to see'. Koltès is a famous French playwright.
Deux places pour mardi?
'Two tickets for Tuesday?' The word for ticket here really means 'seat', as in a seat at the theatre.
Mardi, tu as le film de Kechiche.
'On Tuesday you've got the Kechiche film.' Magali uses the casual 'you' with her boss, and that's normal at ASK. Days of the week need no little word in front of them.
Jeudi, alors.
'Thursday, then.' Andréa decides in a second.
Et demain, tu déjeunes avec Audiard.
'And tomorrow you're having lunch with Audiard.' French has a single verb that means 'to have lunch'. Audiard is a big film director, so Andréa grabs the chance.
Je prends ça. Merci.
'I'll take that. Thanks.' The present tense is enough to say what you're about to do.
Tu déjeunes aussi avec Dany Boon demain.
'You're also having lunch with Dany Boon tomorrow.' The trouble is she already has a lunch with a famous comedian tomorrow.
Tu es pénible, Magali.
'You're a pain, Magali.' Said with a sigh, to the one person keeping her life in order.
L'un à midi, l'autre à quatorze heures.
'One at noon, the other at two.' French offices often use the twenty-four-hour clock, so two in the afternoon is fourteen hours.
Je vais déjeuner deux fois.
'I'm going to have lunch twice.' Here's a handy pattern: the verb 'to go' plus a plain verb gives you the near future, exactly like 'I'm going to' in English.
Appelle Clémentine.
'Call Clémentine.' Now a string of orders in the casual form. Clémentine is a woman Andréa is seeing, and she wants to cancel tonight's date.
Dis-lui que je ne peux pas venir ce soir.
'Tell her I can't come tonight.' The command comes first, joined to the little word for 'to her'. And notice the negative again, wrapped around the verb 'can'.
Clémentine? Celle de la semaine dernière?
'Clémentine? The one from last week?' Magali can't keep up with Andréa's love life.
Il y a une autre Clémentine?
'Is there another Clémentine?' Andréa teases her right back.
Qu'est-ce que je lui dis?
'What do I tell her?' A useful question starter that simply means 'what'.
Je ne sais pas. Trouve quelque chose.
'I don't know. Think of something.' Another casual command: think up, come up with something.
Dis que j'ai une réunion. Improvise!
'Say I've got a meeting. Improvise!' That last word is the same as in English, and it's Andréa's motto. Meanwhile, across the room, Mathias stops at Gabriel's desk.
Gabriel. Tu ne rappelles pas Cécile de France?

'Gabriel. Aren't you calling Cécile de France back?' Cécile has been calling, and Gabriel hasn't picked up. He mumbles that he'll call her. Only we know why he's hiding. Let's hear the morning rush once more, all the way through.
Bonjour! Salut, Mathias.
Oui, trois cent mille. Je parle de ses vingt ans de carrière.
Magali, je dois voir la pièce de Koltès cette semaine.
Deux places pour mardi? Mardi, tu as le film de Kechiche.
Jeudi, alors.
Et demain, tu déjeunes avec Audiard.
Je prends ça. Merci.
Tu déjeunes aussi avec Dany Boon demain.
Tu es pénible, Magali.
L'un à midi, l'autre à quatorze heures. Je vais déjeuner deux fois.
Appelle Clémentine. Dis-lui que je ne peux pas venir ce soir.
Clémentine? Celle de la semaine dernière?
Il y a une autre Clémentine?
Qu'est-ce que je lui dis?
Je ne sais pas. Trouve quelque chose.
Dis que j'ai une réunion. Improvise!
Gabriel. Tu ne rappelles pas Cécile de France?
That's a typical morning at ASK: two lunches, one cancelled date and a lot of casual commands. Don't worry if it felt fast; it is fast, even for the French. See you in the next scene.
Allez, au travail!
